title: How Panic Attacks Work
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant open with a tangent about a Widespread Panic concert attack, then explain panic attacks and panic disorder: prevalence (about 2.8% of Americans), symptoms listed in the DSM, the autonomic nervous system and fight-flight-freeze response, and the NKRT3 gene research. They cover possible causes (genetics, childhood trauma, an overactive fear system, breathing and sodium lactate or CO2 theories, serotonin and GABA), the link to agoraphobia, and treatments: SSRIs, benzodiazepines like Xanax, beta blockers, and CBT with exposure therapy. They describe diaphragmatic breathing exercises, how to help someone having an attack, and how to tell a heart attack apart. The episode closes with a listener email about using the podcast to distract from basement fear, and the sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and Widespread Panic attack
segments.summary: Hosts open with a tangent about a fan attacking the Widespread Panic band on stage, then introduce the topic of panic attacks versus panic disorder and its prevalence.

segments.title: Panic attack basics and the NKRT3 gene
segments.summary: Panic attacks are discussed as an intense fear response with no real danger. Hosts describe a December gene discovery (NKRT3) linked to exaggerated fear, and explain the fight, flight, or freeze response.

segments.title: Symptoms and diagnosis
segments.summary: The DSM symptom list is covered, with at least four symptoms signaling a panic attack. Four attacks in four weeks, or fear of another for a month, can lead to a panic disorder diagnosis.

segments.title: Autonomic nervous system and the panic response
segments.summary: The autonomic nervous system's sympathetic and parasympathetic parts are explained. In a panic attack, adrenaline drives the sympathetic response and the parasympathetic calm-down does not kick in.

segments.title: Causes of panic attacks
segments.summary: Possible causes are discussed: genetics (twin studies), childhood trauma, an overactive fear system, breathing and CO2 or sodium lactate theories, and reduced serotonin receptors and GABA. Demographics are noted, and an evolutionary theory is dismissed.

segments.title: Agoraphobia and phobias
segments.summary: Agoraphobia is explained as almost always resulting from panic disorder, as people come to fear places where attacks happened. Old Freudian explanations are mentioned and rejected.

segments.title: Treatments: medication and therapy
segments.summary: Panic disorder is described as highly treatable, with success rates around sixty percent or more. Treatments covered include SSRIs, benzodiazepines like Xanax, beta blockers, and CBT with exposure therapy and rethinking.

segments.title: Breathing exercises and coping techniques
segments.summary: Coping techniques center on diaphragmatic breathing, including a book-on-stomach exercise and self-talk. Advice is given on helping someone having an attack and on lifestyle changes such as exercise, mindfulness, and cutting caffeine.
topics: helping someone during a panic attack

segments.title: Personal anecdotes and heart attack warning signs
segments.summary: Hosts share stories of a friend and Emily's panic attacks, then list American Heart Association warning signs of a heart attack to distinguish it from a panic attack.

segments.title: Listener mail: basement fear
segments.summary: A listener named Kelsey in Kansas City, Kansas, says she uses Stuff You Should Know episodes on her phone to distract herself from irrational fear of the basement, which she says is a form of exposure therapy.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information for the show and sign off.
